source: Mamede, Schmidt, Penaforte (2008) Effects of reflective practice on the accuracy of medical diagnoses
finding: Founding experiment. Residents diagnosed 16 cases by pattern recognition or reflective reasoning. Reflection helped on complex cases only; on simple cases it made no difference.
numbers: N=42 internal medicine residents (Brazil). Repeated measures. Case complexity x mode interaction F(1,41)=4.48, p<.05. No main effect of reflection.
limits: Abstract read. Written vignettes, one site, Brazil. Complexity defined from prior accuracy data.
agent_relevance: Supports G1: second look has value only when the case is hard. A trigger on difficulty or disagreement is better than a fixed second pass.

source: Mamede, Schmidt (2023) Deliberate reflection and clinical reasoning: founding ideas and empirical findings (Med Educ)
finding: Authors' own 15-year summary. Deliberate reflection (DR) is a fixed written procedure: list findings for, findings against, findings expected but missing, then an alternative hypothesis, repeat, rank. Works for hard cases, not routine ones. Needs knowledge to retrieve. Instructions to be more analytical or to avoid bias did not help.
numbers: Residents' accuracy gained more than 35% with DR on complex cases (replication study). Students were hurt by DR on complex cases but helped on simple ones. Only 23 adequately controlled reflection studies existed per Prakash 2019. Reading unrelated Q-fever or Legionnaire page in morning raised look-alike errors in afternoon; DR after the test restored accuracy.
quote: attempts to be more analytical did not help; in some cases performance even deteriorated
limits: Self-review by the main lab; most evidence comes from this one programme. Vignettes contain all information, no real information gathering. Authors state mechanism is unclear.
agent_relevance: Gives the exact S5/S8 procedure to copy as an operator: for/against/missing-expected per hypothesis, then a new hypothesis. Keep it code-driven and stepwise, not a free instruction to think harder.

source: Prakash, Sladek, Schuwirth (2019) Interventions to improve diagnostic decision making: systematic review and meta-analysis on reflective strategies
finding: Only meta-analysis on reflection. Guided reflection improves diagnosis with a moderate effect. Other interventions could not be pooled because of method problems.
numbers: 44 studies of 10,114 screened, 4380 professionals. Guided reflection effect size 0.38 (95% CI 0.23-0.52), p<0.001.
limits: Abstract read. Mostly students and residents, vignettes, short follow-up. Searches 2000-2016. Publication bias not assessed in abstract.
agent_relevance: A usable prior: guided second look gives about d=0.4 for humans on vignettes. Our agent should not assume more.

source: Lambe, O'Reilly, Kelly, Curristan (2016) Dual-process cognitive interventions to enhance diagnostic reasoning: a systematic review
finding: Guided reflection was the most consistently successful intervention (five studies). Cognitive forcing improved accuracy and confidence judgements in some studies. Measurement methods varied a lot.
numbers: 28 studies in five categories: educational interventions, checklists, cognitive forcing, guided reflection, instructions at test.
limits: Abstract read. Mostly early-career doctors. Narrative synthesis only, no pooled effect.
agent_relevance: Confirms that structured guidance, not generic debiasing talk, is what works.

source: Norman, Sherbino, Dore et al. (2014) The etiology of diagnostic errors: controlled trial of System 1 versus System 2 reasoning
finding: Failed intervention. Telling residents to be slow, careful and reflective gave no accuracy gain over telling them to be fast.
numbers: N=204 second-year residents (96 speed in 2010, 108 reflect in 2011) at McMaster, Ottawa, McGill; 20 cases. Accuracy 44.5% speed vs 45.0% reflect (ns). Time 69 s vs 89 s (p<.001). Wrong cases took 17 s longer in both.
quote: simply encouraging slowing down and increasing attention to analytical thinking is insufficient to increase diagnostic accuracy
limits: Cohorts differ by year, not randomised in the same sitting. Instruction only; no structured procedure. Written cases.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G1 and for 'no persona or instruction to think harder'. A generic 'think carefully' prompt costs tokens and buys nothing.

source: Monteiro, Sherbino, Sibbald, Norman et al. (2015/2016) Reflecting on diagnostic errors: taking a second look is not enough (J Gen Intern Med)
finding: Self-directed second look barely helps. Residents revised only 8% of diagnoses, and accuracy rose from 1.20 to 1.22 out of 2.
numbers: N=47 residents (PGY1-3), 16 cases. Revised at least one: 12/19 PGY1, 9/11 PGY2, 8/17 PGY3. Gain t=2.15, p=0.03.
quote: this strategy provided minimal benefits compared to knowing the correct answer
limits: Participant chose whether to reflect and gave no structured procedure. Gain is statistically small and practically tiny.
agent_relevance: A free 'check your answer' pass with no signal and no new evidence gives close to nothing. Matches Huang 2023 for LLMs.

source: Mamede, Hautz, Berendonk et al. (2020) Think twice: returning to the case to reflect upon the initial diagnosis (Acad Med)
finding: On very hard cases a second look raised accuracy by a small amount, and the kind of reflection did not matter: no instruction, confirming evidence, contradicting evidence, or both all gave the same gain.
numbers: N=167 physicians (Swiss internal medicine exam). Accuracy 0.22 to 0.26 overall (p<.001). Groups final: no instruction 0.23, confirm 0.31, contradict 0.26, both 0.25; group differences ns. Baseline was only about 22%.
limits: Floor effect: most physicians were wrong at first. Gain small (4 points). Structured for/against search not better than plain return to the case.
agent_relevance: Competing finding to the DR procedure: simply re-reading the case may deliver most of the gain. Test arms: plain re-read vs for/against table at equal tokens.

source: Ilgen, Bowen, McIntyre et al. (2013) Comparing diagnostic performance under conditions to encourage automatic or analytic thought (Acad Med)
finding: Failed replication of the analytic advantage. Directed search (list three likely diagnoses and evidence for and against each) did not beat first impression.
numbers: N=393 clinicians (students, trainees, faculty), multicentre RCT. Instruction effect F(1,379)=2.44, p=.12. Complexity F=965, experience F=39.6.
limits: Hypotheses were generated before the evidence review (top-down), which Mamede and Schmidt say is not the DR procedure. First-impression condition gave more reliable assessment scores.
agent_relevance: Shows order matters. Generate the answer first, then examine it against the findings. Forcing a list of rivals up front did not help.

source: Mamede, Schmidt (2014) Reflection in diagnostic reasoning: what really matters? (Acad Med)
finding: Reply to Ilgen 2013. Argues the DR procedure requires hypotheses to emerge one at a time from confronting findings, so Ilgen's top-down version is a different thing.
numbers: No new data. Cited in Mamede and Schmidt 2023 as the rebuttal.
limits: Only the PubMed record and the 2023 review's description were seen. Not opened.
agent_relevance: A competing explanation, not tested head to head. Worth a direct arm in our tests: sequential vs list-first.

source: Kulatunga-Moruzi, Brooks, Norman (2011) Teaching posttraining: influencing diagnostic strategy with instructions at test (J Exp Psychol Appl)
finding: Instructions at test can shift students between analytic and similarity-based processing. Dual instructions (similarity first, rules second) improved accuracy. Rules first can inhibit the similarity step.
numbers: Two studies with medical students. Typicality effect indexes analytic use, similarity effect indexes pattern use.
limits: Abstract read; no sample sizes in abstract. Students with trained categories, not clinicians.
agent_relevance: Supports ordering: fast match first, then rule check. Matches the schema idea of an attempt followed by a check.

source: Eva, Hatala, LeBlanc, Brooks (2007) Teaching from the clinical reasoning literature: combined reasoning strategies (Med Educ)
finding: Combined instruction (pattern recognition plus careful consideration of features) beat no instruction, most strongly when cases were made misleading.
numbers: Study 1 N=60, Study 2 N=48 psychology undergraduates trained on 10 ECG diagnoses.
limits: Novice undergraduates, ECGs. Not physicians.
agent_relevance: Combined strategy is the same shape as a quick answer then a check against the findings.

source: Mamede, van Gog, van den Berge et al. (2010) Availability bias and reflective reasoning in internal medicine residents (JAMA)
finding: Recent exposure to similar cases caused errors in second-year residents (availability bias). Reflection after the first diagnosis raised accuracy in both years.
numbers: N=36 residents (18 R1, 18 R2). R2 accuracy 1.55 on similar cases vs 2.19 on others (p=.03). R1 showed the reverse (2.03 vs 1.42, p=.046). Reflection on similar cases: R2 2.03, R1 2.31; mode effect p=.006. Out of 4.0.
limits: Small sample. Bias effect inconsistent across years. Reflection step is a repeat of the same cases, so gain could include a second-look effect.
agent_relevance: Reflection recovers anchoring caused by recent context. Relevant for an agent with long context carrying earlier cases.

source: Mamede, Splinter, van Gog, Rikers, Schmidt (2012) Salient distracting features and how reflection counteracts mistakes (BMJ Qual Saf)
finding: Secondary analysis: reflection fixed errors caused by salient distracting features, but only for residents. Students did not gain.
numbers: Residents (n=34) reflective M=2.09 vs non-analytic M=1.71 (p=0.03). Errors from salient features 0.47 vs 0.85 (p=0.02). Students (n=50) no benefit.
limits: Secondary analysis; error cause was coded by five internists after the fact.
agent_relevance: Mechanism hint: reflection redirects attention from a seductive cue to discriminating cues. Needs the knowledge to see which cues discriminate.

source: Schmidt, van Gog, Schuit et al. (2017) Do patients' disruptive behaviours influence diagnostic accuracy? (BMJ Qual Saf)
finding: Patient disruptive behaviour lowered accuracy and reflection corrected it (as summarised in the 2023 review).
numbers: Numbers not read; the 2023 review reports errors were corrected after deliberate reflection in two randomised studies (Schmidt 2017, Mamede 2017).
limits: Only title and a secondary description seen. Not opened.
agent_relevance: Context noise (tone, affect in the prompt) can be repaired by a second look; test with emotional or hostile case wording.

source: Mamede, de Carvalho, de Faria et al. (2020) 'Immunising' physicians against availability bias (BMJ Qual Saf)
finding: Content knowledge beat process: one week after comparing look-alike diseases with feedback, physicians resisted a bias-inducing exposure. Knowledge, not reasoning style, protected them.
numbers: N=91 second-year residents, 8 hospitals. Subjected-to-bias vignettes: immunised 0.40 vs 0.24 (difference 0.16, 95% CI 0.05-0.27, p=0.004). Not-subjected: 0.36 vs 0.41 (ns).
limits: Simulated vignettes, one-week gap, two disease clusters.
agent_relevance: Strong support that S5 revise needs retrieved discriminating knowledge (contrast tables), not just more reasoning steps.

source: Mamede, Goeijenbier, Schuit et al. (2020/21) Specific disease knowledge as predictor of susceptibility to availability bias (J Gen Intern Med)
finding: Residents who knew the discriminating features were less biased, and extra reflection helped only if they had that knowledge.
numbers: N=62. Biased diagnoses: higher knowledge 0.35 vs lower knowledge 0.97 (difference 0.62, 95% CI 0.28-0.95, p=0.001). Both groups took longer on bias-exposed cases (p=0.04).
limits: Knowledge measured by a 2-second feature-association task. Simulated setting.
agent_relevance: Second look cannot create knowledge the model lacks. For the agent, pair the revise step with retrieval, not self-talk.

source: Sherbino, Kulasegaram, Howey, Norman (2014) Ineffectiveness of cognitive forcing strategies to reduce biases in diagnostic reasoning (CJEM)
finding: Failed intervention. Teaching cognitive forcing strategies for four weeks did not reduce search-satisficing or availability errors.
numbers: N=191 students (145 trained, 46 control). Second diagnosis found: 54% vs 48% (p=.13). Uncommon diagnosis in availability cases: 45% in both groups (p=.98). Oversearching on false-positive cases 64% vs 77% (ns).
limits: Novices; training lasted a rotation; test was computer cases.
agent_relevance: Awareness of bias and slogans do not transfer. Do not add 'watch for anchoring' prompts.

source: Kaemmer, Schauber, Hautz, Stroben, Hautz (2021) Differential diagnosis checklists reduce diagnostic error differentially (Med Educ)
finding: A checklist of 17 diagnoses helped only if it contained the right answer. If it lacked the answer accuracy fell below control.
numbers: N=90 advanced students, six cases. Accuracy 0.75 (checklist with correct dx) vs 0.49 control vs 0.43 (checklist without correct dx; ns vs control). Time per case 3:52 and 4:20 vs 2:59 min.
limits: Students, computer cases. Checklist contents are knowledge, not process.
agent_relevance: Supplying alternatives helps only when the right one is in the set. Echoes G4/G5: do not trust the candidate list as complete.

source: Costa Filho, Moura, Brandao, Schmidt, Mamede (2019) Deliberate reflection on diagnostic accuracy, confidence and calibration in dermatology (Perspect Med Educ)
finding: Reflection raised accuracy on image-based dermatology cases but did not change confidence or calibration.
numbers: N=61 sixth-year students, 12 images. Accuracy 49.7 +/- 12.1 vs 38.4 +/- 14.6 (p=0.002). Confidence 64.3 vs 58.9 (p=0.228). Calibration 0.15 vs 0.20 (p=0.197). Overconfidence rose with difficulty (p<0.001).
limits: Students not physicians, control did a time-filler task. Extends reflection to visual tasks.
agent_relevance: Reflection does not fix confidence. So do not use model self-confidence after a second look as a trust signal (G3, G5).

source: Mamede, van Gog, Moura et al. (2012) Reflection as a strategy to foster students' acquisition of diagnostic competence (Med Educ)
finding: Learning, not performance: structured reflection while practising cases hurt at once but helped a week later.
numbers: N=46 Year 4. Immediate test: reflection 0.48 vs differential 0.62 (p=0.012) and immediate dx 0.61. One week later: reflection 0.66 vs 0.48 and 0.52 (p<.01 and p=.01).
limits: Learning-phase effect; not about in-the-moment diagnosis.
agent_relevance: Little relevance to a single inference; relevant if lessons are stored for later cases (a replay or memory step).

source: Mamede, van Gog, Sampaio et al. (2014) How can students' diagnostic competence benefit most from practice with clinical cases? (Acad Med)
finding: Replication of the delayed-learning benefit, with transfer to adjacent diseases.
numbers: N=110 Year 4 students. One week later new exemplars: reflection 0.67 vs single dx 0.36 (p<.001) vs differential 0.51 (p=.014). New adjacent diseases: 0.44 vs 0.32 (p=.010) and 0.33 (p=.015).
limits: Same lab, same population type. No independent lab replication in the set I found.
agent_relevance: Reflection on contrasts can change stored knowledge, hinting at a use in the agent's lesson store.

source: Ibiapina, Mamede, Moura, Eloi-Santos, van Gog (2014) Free, cued and modelled reflection (Med Educ)
finding: Guidance beat free reflection: telling students which diagnoses to reflect on, or showing worked reflection, did better and cost less effort.
numbers: N=115 (58 Year 5, 57 Year 6). Cued and modelled equal (p=1.00), both better than free (p<0.001).
limits: Students; test cases drawn from the studied diseases.
agent_relevance: Unguided self-reflection is the weakest form. Give the revise step a template and a cue (the specific hypothesis to test).

source: Mamede, Figueiredo-Soares, Santos, de Faria, Schmidt, van Gog (2019) Fostering novice students' diagnostic ability: guiding deliberate reflection (Med Educ)
finding: Replicated Ibiapina in novices: cued reflection beat free reflection on studied diseases; no gain on adjacent diseases.
numbers: N=80 third-year students. Studied diseases: cued 0.58 (SD 0.23) vs free 0.41 (SD 0.20), p<0.02; modelled 0.54. Adjacent diseases: all three near floor, ns.
limits: Transfer finding in Mamede 2014 did not replicate for novices (floor effect).
agent_relevance: Boundary: transfer to neighbours needs prior knowledge.

source: Fernandes, Malloy-Diniz, de Vasconcellos, Camargos, Ibiapina (2021) Adding guidance to deliberate reflection improves students' diagnostic accuracy (Med Educ)
finding: Independent group replicated guidance benefit; for complex cases the delayed benefit held only for senior students.
numbers: N=80 third-year plus 62 sixth-year students; cued and worked example did not differ and both beat free reflection (p<.001). Complex cases delayed benefit only in seniors (p<.001).
limits: Brazilian students again; Ibiapina is a co-author of the earlier study so partly the same network.
agent_relevance: Expertise moderates: weaker knowledge, less gain on hard cases.

source: Mamede, Schmidt, Rikers, Custers, Splinter, van Saase (2010) Conscious thought beats deliberation without attention in diagnostic decision-making: at least when you are an expert (Psychol Res)
finding: Experts gained from conscious thought on complex problems; novices gained from unconscious delay only on simple problems and did not gain from thinking on complex ones.
numbers: Doctors and students, complex and routine problems, three conditions (immediate, conscious thought, unconscious thought). No effect on simple problems for experts.
limits: Abstract read; sample sizes not in abstract.
agent_relevance: Expertise by difficulty interaction: thinking more helps only if the thinker has relevant knowledge.

source: Mamede et al. (2008) Influence of perceived difficulty of cases on physicians' diagnostic reasoning; and (2007) Breaking down automaticity (Med Educ)
finding: Physicians shift into reflection on their own when they perceive a case as problematic, and accuracy rises. Telling them others had failed the case was enough to trigger it.
numbers: Exp 1: 20 residents, 10 cases; accuracy higher in the problematic context. Exp 2: 18 residents think-aloud; more time, memory and inferences. Ambiguity study (2007): 16 residents, ambiguous cases slower and less accurate (recall t(15)=2.29, p=.037).
limits: Small samples. Trigger was a manipulation, not a natural signal.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for G1: a perceived-difficulty signal can switch on reflection and helps. Our code-detected signals (disagreement, failed check) play that role.

source: Mamede, Schmidt (2023) unresolved issues section: second pass alone and vignette limits
finding: Authors note that a second pass over the case alone matched DR gains (Think Twice), so the lengthy written procedure may not be needed. Also the DR benefit was shown only on vignettes that contain all information.
numbers: No new numbers; cites Mamede 2020 (N=167).
limits: Review claim; not independent.
agent_relevance: Cheap second-look arm is a real competitor; measure it at equal tokens.

source: Norman et al. (2012) The relationship between response time and diagnostic accuracy (Acad Med)
finding: Faster answers were more accurate, not less. Slow does not mean right.
numbers: N=75 graduates, 25 cases. Correlation of response time with accuracy -0.54. Held in 23 of 25 cases and with knowledge controlled.
limits: Time is confounded with difficulty and knowledge.
agent_relevance: Do not read long deliberation as evidence of quality; extra thinking tokens correlate with hardness, not with correctness.

source: Huang, Chen, Mishra, Zheng, Yu, Song, Zhou (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet (ICLR 2024)
finding: Without outside feedback, asking an LLM to review and fix its answer lowers accuracy. Gains in earlier papers came from using the gold label to decide when to stop.
numbers: GPT-3.5: GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 (round 1) and 74.7 (round 2); CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 and 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 to 25.0. GPT-4: GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 and 89.0; CSQA 82.0 to 79.5 and 80.0; HotpotQA 49.0 to 49.0 and 43.0. With oracle labels: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3, CSQA 75.8 to 89.7, HotpotQA 26.0 to 29.0; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 97.5, CSQA 82.0 to 85.5, HotpotQA 49.0 to 59.0. GPT-4-Turbo GSM8K 91.5 to 88.0/90.0. Llama-2 GSM8K 62.0 to 43.5/36.5. GPT-3.5 kept its answer 74.7% of the time on GSM8K and flipped correct to wrong more than wrong to correct.
limits: General reasoning benchmarks, not medicine. Table text extracted by pdftotext was scrambled in places; oracle rows should be rechecked against the paper. 2023 models.
agent_relevance: The strongest LLM analogue of 'taking a second look is not enough': intrinsic revision hurts. Matches schema G2: revise only from real output and external signal.

source: Kamoi, Zhang, Zhang, Han, Zhang (2024) When can LLMs actually correct their own mistakes? A critical survey (TACL)
finding: No prior work shows successful self-correction from prompted-LLM feedback, except on tasks exceptionally suited to it. Self-correction works where reliable external feedback exists, and with large-scale fine-tuning.
numbers: Survey; no pooled numbers in the page read.
limits: Only the arXiv abstract page was read, not the full paper.
agent_relevance: Same boundary as medical reflection: the reviewer needs new information or a verifier; otherwise skip it.

source: Exposing the fragility of LLM reasoning through bias-inducing prompts (BMJ Digit Health AI)
finding: Reasoning variants beat base models on accuracy but were not consistently less biased. A debiasing prompt and few-shot examples did reduce biased answers in all three models.
numbers: 1273 vignettes, 7 biases. Reasoning vs base: Llama-3.3-70B 72.5-82.1% vs 61.0-73.4%; Qwen3-32B 71.7-78.7% vs 55.5-64.1%; Gemini-2.5-Flash 81.8-88.6% vs 80.0-83.7%. Gemini fell from 80.0-88.6% to 47.4-86.1% on four unpublished bias prompts.
limits: Multiple-choice vignettes; debiasing prompt is an instruction, which for humans failed. Possible training contamination.
agent_relevance: Instruction-type debiasing works for LLMs where it fails for humans, but only on the stated bias. Longer reasoning is not a defence.

source: Cognitively biased prompt effects on LLM accuracy for radiology board-style questions (2026, Radiol Artif Intell)
finding: Authority, complexity and anchoring cues in the prompt cut accuracy in ten LLMs. A prompt bias audit and a one-shot mitigation recovered part of it.
numbers: 10 LLMs, 200 text and 200 multimodal questions. Baseline 84.8% text, 59.5% multimodal. Drops: authority -21.1 and -44.9 points; complexity -10.1 and -44.4; anchoring -4.4 and -39.6. Audit +5.6 text, +15.8 multimodal; one-shot +4.0 and +24.9.
limits: Board-style questions, not real cases. Mitigation recovers only a fraction.
agent_relevance: LLMs show the anchoring that DR was built to fix. A separate check pass that sees the case without the stated answer (G5) is the analogue of 'return to the findings'.

source: Multi-agent conversations to mitigate cognitive biases in clinical decision-making (2024, J Med Internet Res)
finding: GPT-4 agents with a devil's advocate, expert and facilitator turned initial misdiagnoses into a correct top-2 differential most of the time.
numbers: 16 case reports with known bias-driven misdiagnoses, 5 repeats, 240 responses. Initial diagnosis accuracy 0/80. Best framework top-2 accuracy 76% (61/80), vs humans OR 3.49, p=.002.
limits: Cases are published misdiagnoses so first-pass accuracy is 0 by selection. No no-agent second-pass control at equal tokens. Same model plays all roles, so G4 applies.
agent_relevance: Evidence that a structured challenge can break anchoring on hard cases, but the missing equal-effort control is exactly what we must supply.

source: Simulated reasoning and self-verification for psychiatric diagnosis in generalist LLMs (2026, JMIR AI)
finding: Adding a self-verification prompt raised precision of diagnoses without changing sensitivity, even on reasoning models.
numbers: 106 DSM-5-TR vignettes, two LLMs and two reasoning models (OpenAI, Google). Sensitivity 0.732-0.817 (no effect). PPV 0.534-0.779; effect of self-verification p=.007, reasoning model p=.009. Best: o3-pro with self-verification, sensitivity 0.782, PPV 0.779.
limits: Vignettes from a textbook, likely seen in training. Self-verification prompts were hand-written, effects on PPV only.
agent_relevance: Verification trims false positives but does not find missed diagnoses: use it as a filter in S8, not as a search for new answers.

source: Reflective self-review vs single agent for code-status extraction from notes (2026, JAMIA)
finding: For capable models self-reflection and a reviewer agent did not help and sometimes hurt; only a weak 8B model gained from a reviewer.
numbers: 1000 MIMIC-IV notes, 4 open models. Reflective self-review impaired MedGemma-27B on DNI extraction (p=.047). Multi-agent review doubled tokens and latency without accuracy gains. DeepSeek-R1-Distill-8B gained for DNR (p=.017) and CMO (p<.001).
limits: Extraction, not diagnosis. Easy explicit labels, so the Mamede difficulty boundary applies.
agent_relevance: Capability-by-difficulty interaction repeats in LLMs: a second look helps weak solvers on hard items, hurts or wastes on easy ones.

source: Ribeiro, Mamede et al. (2021) Exploring mechanisms underlying learning from deliberate reflection (Med Educ)
finding: Replication that reflection on cases boosts later learning from a text, mainly by a cognitive mechanism, with a motivational contribution.
numbers: N=101 fifth-year students. Recall 72.56 vs 58.80 (p=.01); interest 4.45 vs 3.99 (p<.001); awareness of gaps 4.13 vs 3.85 (p<.01). No interaction with study time.
limits: Learning outcome, not diagnosis.
agent_relevance: Weak relevance; shows the gap-awareness effect, which an agent might mimic by listing what is missing.

source: Case revisitation during deliberate reflection (2026, Diagnosis (Berl))
finding: Whether the case stays visible during reflection changes what is learned: hiding it helped studied diseases, showing it helped adjacent diseases. No overall difference.
numbers: N=67 third and fourth-year students, 15-day delay. Interaction chi2(1)=7.68, p=0.006. Studied diseases without access OR=1.77 (95% CI 0.76-2.78, p=0.050); adjacent diseases with access OR=0.56 (95% CI 0.24-0.89, p=0.050). Confidence OR=1.12, recall OR=1.06.
limits: Borderline p-values. Students. Learning, not in-the-moment diagnosis. Reported CIs look inconsistent with the ORs as quoted, treat the numbers cautiously.
agent_relevance: Whether the reviewer sees the original text or only its own notes is a testable design choice for S8.

source: Mamede, Schmidt, Rikers et al. replication set summary: reflection by case difficulty and expertise (Med Educ 2023 review, ref 18)
finding: In a second study, residents improved by more than 35% with DR on hard cases and gained nothing on simple ones, while students gained on simple cases and did worse on hard ones.
numbers: Residents +35% relative accuracy on complex cases; students: benefit on simple, worse on complex.
limits: Relative gain as reported by the authors; raw figures not in the review text.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition for scaling: a small or weak model may be hurt by reflection on hard items.
